title: Whose voice?
goal: Say what inversion does in prose and poetry, and recognize and write free indirect speech.

intro.text: Writers move words after the verb for rhythm and emphasis: *Uyuyordu kasaba.* And they let a character think inside the narrator's sentences, with no quotation marks and no *diye*: *Yarın gidiyordu. Ne yapacaktı şimdi?* This is free indirect speech.

vocab.en: style (of a writer or a text)
to drift off (into thought); to dive
hope (accusative: umudu; umut etmek: to hope)

exercises.question: In *Uyuyordu kasaba.*, why does *kasaba* come after the verb?
options: The town is the known setting; the sentence lingers on it at the end
The town is the focus: the town, and nothing else, was asleep
It is a mistake: the verb must come last
It turns the sentence into a question

why.1: The focus goes right before the verb ([C1 unit 6](gp-focus-position)); after the verb comes what is already known.
why.2: Inversion is normal in narration, dialogue and poetry.
why.3: A question would need *mI* or a question word.

exercises.explain: After the verb comes background, and in literature also what the writer wants to leave in the reader's ear: the image of the sleeping town.

exercises.prompt: Uyuyordu kasaba; yalnız denizin sesi duyuluyordu.
accept: The town was asleep; only the sound of the sea could be heard.
The town was asleep; only the sound of the sea was heard
The town was asleep; only the sound of the sea was audible
The town was sleeping; only the sound of the sea [could be heard|was heard|was audible]
The town was [asleep|sleeping], and only the sound of the sea [could be heard|was heard|was audible]
The town was [asleep|sleeping]; all [you|one] could hear was the sound of the sea
Asleep was the town; only the sound of the sea could be heard
exercises.explain: English can keep the subject first; *Asleep was the town* imitates the inversion but sounds more marked than the Turkish.

exercises.question: Which sentence puts the first half of this couplet by Ziya Paşa into prose order?

context.tr: Âyinesi iştir kişinin lafa bakılmaz / Şahsın görünür rütbe-i aklı eserinde
context.en: A person's mirror is their work; words count for nothing. / The rank of a person's mind shows in what they make.

why.1: The line says the opposite: *lafa bakılmaz*, one doesn't look at words.
why.2: *İş kişinin aynasıdır* is a fair paraphrase, but *aynaya bakılmaz* changes the second half: it is words that don't count.

exercises.explain: *Âyine* is the old word for *ayna*. The metre and the rhyme put the predicate *iştir* in the middle of the possessive phrase *kişinin âyinesi*.

exercises.en: Ayşe looked out of the window. She was leaving tomorrow.

accept: gidiyordu

reject.why: In free indirect speech the narrator keeps the third person and the past: *gidiyordu*. *Gidiyorum* would need quotation marks and *diye*.
*Gideceğini* needs a verb of thinking or saying after it; free indirect speech has none.
The story is told in the past (*baktı*), so her thought moves into the past too: *gidiyordu*.

exercises.hint: Ayşe thinks *Yarın gidiyorum*. Keep her *yarın*, but tell it in the narrator's person and tense.
exercises.explain: Her own word *yarın* stays; person and tense are the narrator's: *Yarın gidiyordu.*

exercises.prompt: What was she going to do now?
accept: Ne yapacaktı şimdi?
Şimdi ne yapacaktı?
O şimdi ne yapacaktı?
Şimdi o ne yapacaktı?
Ne yapacaktı o şimdi?

reject.why: That is a thought in the present. In a past story it moves to the future in the past: *Ne yapacaktı şimdi?*

exercises.explain: The future in the past `-(y)AcAktI` is the tense of a character's questions about what comes next. *Şimdi* after the verb gives the free indirect rhythm.

exercises.question: Which of these is free indirect speech?
options: Saat ona geliyordu. Annesi yine kızacaktı, belliydi.

why.1: Direct speech: the character's words in quotation marks, with *diye*.
why.2: Indirect speech: a noun clause and a verb of thinking.
why.3: Plain narration of an event: there is no thought here.

exercises.explain: Third person and past (*kızacaktı*), but the character's own worry and her *belliydi*: free indirect speech.

exercises.prompt: Kardeşi yine geç kalmıştı. Çok önemli bir işi varmış!
accept: Her brother was late again. He had something very important to do, apparently!
Her brother was late again. He had something really important to do, apparently!
Her brother had been late again. He had something [very|really] important to do, apparently!
His brother [was|had been] late again. He had something [very|really] important to do, apparently!
[Her|His] brother [was|had been] late again. Apparently he had something [very|really] important to do!
[Her|His] brother [was|had been] late again. [Supposedly|So|It seems] he had something [very|really] important to do!
[Her|His] sister [was|had been] late again. She had something [very|really] important to do, apparently!
[Her|His] sister [was|had been] late again. [Apparently|Supposedly|So|It seems] she had something [very|really] important to do!
[Her|His] brother [was|had been] late again. He had [some|a] very important business, apparently!
exercises.explain: *Varmış*: the narrator repeats the brother's excuse and keeps her distance from it; the exclamation mark adds the irony. English **apparently** or **supposedly** does the same.

exercises.task: Rewrite in free indirect speech: keep the third person and the past, drop the quotation marks and *diye düşündü*, and keep Elif's own words and her question.
exercises.source: Elif mektubu okudu. “Demek her şey bitti. Şimdi ne yapacağım?” diye düşündü.
models: Elif mektubu okudu. Demek her şey bitmişti. Şimdi ne yapacaktı?
Elif mektubu bir kez daha okudu. Her şey bitmişti demek. Ne yapacaktı şimdi?
checklist: No quotation marks and no *diye düşündü*
Elif's own words stay: *demek*, *şimdi* and the question mark
Optional: a word after the verb for rhythm, as in *Ne yapacaktı şimdi?*

exercises.tr: Ne bir ses vardı ne bir ışık.
exercises.en: There was neither a sound nor a light.
options: Ne bir ses vardı ne bir ışık.
Ne bir ses vardı ne bir kuş.
Hem bir ses vardı hem bir ışık.

exercises.prompt: We walked, all the way to morning. (Literary order: the verb first.)
